intro: Everything that happens in the hackathon lands here, newest on top. Every working session is recorded and numbered: S01, S02 and so on. All times are Prague (CET).

posts.title: What's being built today
Research gets its first lists

blocks.text: The research agent drafts five research lists: one for the whole project, and one each for scraping, the blog pipeline, outbound and the brand assets. Each list ends with three "wildcard" questions that Alex puts to every plan: can it be executed, can it be delivered, and will it be received? The project-wide list is waiting for Alex's approval. Two of the questions it proposes:

items: How do the strongest "job application as outreach" sites make the work clear to a non-technical decision maker in under a minute?
What tips a personalised website built as a job application from impressive to creepy, and what makes the recipient act on it?

blocks.text: Once he approves, one agent per question researches it, all in parallel.

posts.title: The finish line is defined

blocks.text: The orchestration session drafts the project's definition of done: 22 items, each something a person who wasn't there could check tomorrow morning. Two examples: "three blog posts are live on the site", and "the site shows every deliverable and its status". Alex signs it off at 14:02 with one change: research no longer needs his approval at every step.

Then the project orchestrator builds its tools. It can add a deliverable in one step, change the plan or the definition of done, and push every change to everything that depends on it. Its consistency check was tested on a scratch copy of the project with seven faults planted in it, and it caught all seven.

posts.title: The first tooling piece is done

blocks.text: Bootstrap finishes. Every piece of work now has its folder, its instructions and its place on the session roster, and bootstrap hands over to the orchestration session, which launches the rest.

posts.title: The demos get their folders

blocks.text: The bootstrap agent creates a working folder for every demo. The agents that build them launch next.

posts.title: It looks quiet, but it isn't

blocks.text: A two-minute video update at about 13:30. AI work is front-loaded, so for the first hours it can look as if nothing is happening. By now the project charter is written: the goals and everything that has to be delivered today.

Agents are breaking each deliverable into a plan they can carry out on their own, including researching how to do it and asking Alex for his judgment where they need it. His goal is to finish everything that needs him by the end of the working day, so the rest runs overnight and he cleans up in the morning.

posts.summary_line: A two-minute status update: the screen looks quiet because the agents are working.

posts.title: The agents take over, and one big mistake

blocks.text: The plan moves from the chat app to the terminal. An orchestration session takes the charter. Three agents write the three tooling specs in parallel, and the answer desk opens. Alex answers each spec's opening questions in one batch, so the agents can carry on without him.
Then, at 13:20, he tries to close one background session he no longer needs, and closes all of them instead.

I just accidentally ended a bunch of sessions, background sessions, they're all working in parallel. I meant to just delete one I didn't need, and turns out if you do that command on the folder, it deletes all of them.

A recovery session brought every session back by about 13:27, each under its old name with its full history. Each one got a note saying exactly where it had stopped and what to pick up. The recording never stopped (the rig and both recorders survived), and nothing that had been committed was lost. Because every session commits its work as it goes, the rest of the project carried on. By 13:50 the fix was saved as recovery scripts in the project, so the next time (a power cut, another wrong click) it's one step.
Hopefully it can spin up all the sessions that were working and just resume, and this is just a 15-minute setback and not an hour-and-a-half setback.

posts.title: The deliverables, and why go slow at the start

blocks.text: Alex lists the ten demos in the status board above. One of them is an agent that watches these recordings and keeps this website up to date, which is how much of this feed gets here. He also explains why he spends the first hours planning instead of building.

Mistakes cascade and they just snowball. You really want to take the time to get it right, because time is no longer the bottleneck, because you can have 20 agents running side by side. The bottleneck is focus. The bottleneck is judgment, discernment.

posts.title: Writing the plan every agent works from

blocks.text: Alex writes the project charter with Claude: the goal, the deliverables, and the rules every agent follows. The rules include the movie-actor rule (everything that needs him gets done first) and one "answer desk" window for all of the agents' questions. In between, he takes a break to talk to the humans watching.
Read the project charter

The progress of learning AI is not the files you have in your computer. It's the clarity of understanding of how all this stuff works … it's clarity. And then the opposite of that is the ability to clearly share that clarity with the assistant.

posts.title: Why this hackathon exists
posts.summary_line: Why this hackathon exists: a job application built live, in public, in one day.

posts.title: Recording starts

blocks.text: Alex switches on a recording rig he built the night before and starts with the first thing followers need: this website. The code is in a public repo from the first commit.
I've never done this screen recording before, but good time to start is when you're under pressure and you've got a 12-hour live project to do.

posts.title: Sizing specs so agents never lose context

blocks.text: While writing the charter, Alex sets the rule for how big each spec should be. Specs are split along topic lines ("semantic cohesion"), and each is run by one orchestrator session that hands as much as it can to subagents and forks at planned points, so its context stays focused through long unattended runs. Then he asks for specs a little smaller than that limit, so more of them can run in parallel.

Passing off as much as possible to sub-agents so that its context window stays semantically clustered and highly usable, and with strategic forking to make sure that there's no context rot for long-term automated work.

posts.title: The three tribes of AI practitioners

blocks.text: Between dictations, Alex lays out his theory that skilled AI practitioners come from one of three tribes. Academics know security but are the least hands-on with commercial AI. Former developers are strong on the deterministic toolkit. Marketers and entrepreneurs like him start with gaps, but bring a fresh view of what's possible and already know go-to-market, where he thinks the need will be. It's also why someone with his CV has to do something like this hackathon to get noticed.

Then you have the former devs who got into AI from coding … they know how to read code and write code. Turned out that's pretty useful for this kind of stuff … a little bit less required than them or the academics would believe, but still more required than the marketers out there think.

posts.title: When the operator is away, agents decide

blocks.text: Alex adds a rule from earlier projects to the charter: a question waiting on him must never stall a build. If a session gets no answer in about 15 minutes, it assumes he's away and makes the call itself, then records the decision, why it's right, and the blast radius if it has to be undone. The agents keep moving, and every judgment call can be reviewed later.
If you don't get a response for 10 minutes, let's say 15 minutes, assume the operator is AFK. And then you get to make the decision.

posts.title: The micromanagement pendulum

blocks.text: Partway through dictating how every working folder should be laid out, Alex stops himself. He describes a swing he keeps going through: you learn you can give an agent the what and let it work out the how, but after a few rounds the results are worse than when you micromanaged, so you swing back. This time he picks the what: each session gets a good reading list, and the agents set up their own folders.

You realize that basically you can just tell it the what and let it figure out the how, but then you let it do that a couple times and realize that it's a lot worse than if you micromanaged it, and then you just kind of get in this weird pendulum.

posts.title: A bad gut feeling, and pressing on

blocks.text: Alex finishes the charter draft in the desktop app instead of his usual terminal setup, and admits he has a bad feeling about it: it's split in a way he wouldn't normally choose, and denser than he'd actually read. His rule is that a bad start is almost always worth restarting, but he judges this one not bad enough, with too little time to spare. To limit the risk, he has the agent mark the charter as a rough draft and give the project orchestrator the final sign-off on the specs and the definition of done.

If you don't like the way something starts and you get a bad feeling about it … it's almost always worth starting over … this is one of the key decisions. I don't think it's bad enough that I need to start over and I don't think I have time to start over.

posts.title: Merges shouldn't wait for Alex's breaks

blocks.text: With several agent sessions about to work in the same repository, Alex needs a rule for when their work gets merged. His first idea, merging whenever he stops the recording, he drops on the spot: his breaks say nothing about whether the agents are done. Instead he asks for a watcher session that merges when everything is idle, or every hour or so, and has a subagent research the best way to do it.

Maybe … when the rig stops we try to … merge everything to main. Well no … never mind, because those don't correlate, because that's just when I'm taking a break or when I need to be away from the computer. That doesn't mean that the assistants are done working.

posts.title: One question per agent in the queue

blocks.text: While setting up the answer desk, the single window where every background session sends its questions, Alex adds a queue rule: each session gets one question waiting at a time, because the answer to one can change the next. That way whatever reaches him is still current. A few minutes later he splits the channel: each spec's opening questions come as one batch he can answer in one go, and the desk is kept for questions that come up along the way.

Only one question per session should be in the queue because the answer to the previous question might change the next question … we need to make sure that anything that hits the answer desk is still current by the time that I'm interacting with it.

posts.title: Research comes before the method

blocks.text: Answering the research spec's opening questions, Alex explains where research sits in his method. Each deliverable first gets its definition of done. Then, before anyone designs how to get there, research checks whether there's already a settled answer, or at least which traps to avoid. Findings go onto the reading list of every spec that needs them, and every research list ends with three wildcard questions.

Make sure that if there's an easy answer, an obvious answer, converged upon answer, we're using it, or if not that we at least know traps and gotchas that we don't fall into. So that when we design the methodology to go from problem to DoD that we have research to guide that process. We're not just using raw training data.

posts.title: Alex builds himself a control room

blocks.text: With a dozen agents running, Alex spends S07 making the project easier to steer instead of building more of it.

points.text: It isn't in the plan. It watches every session every few minutes, so that when he's lost it can tell him where things stand and where he's the blocker.

quote.text: That's going to be the session where I go to where I'm like, I'm lost, there's a million things happening, keep me updated.

points.text: He asks for the agent that reads these recordings and keeps the site updated, started straight away instead of later in the day. That agent wrote this post.

quote.text: Done equals that I just build and work and the website gets additions … I wanted to proactively keep updating the website to show as much as possible to people following along, without me explicitly saying so.
Whatever you did to make all this working again was perfect. Please go ahead and codify that as a skill, so that if I need to use it again, it's an instant fix.

points.text: Anything that waits on Alex becomes a file with an "I approve" box. The waiting agent checks it every five minutes, and the answer desk tells him it's there.

blocks.text: He ends on one priority:
I am going to start this research. And I'm not going to start anything else until that's done.

posts.title: API keys never move on camera

blocks.text: Before the research can start, the project needs API keys, and everything on screen is recorded and published. So Alex stops the recording before he moves them, and gives the agent doing the move a rule: no keys move while the rig is recording.

I'm going to definitely turn off recording while I push, pull all the secret keys over, just in case … Do not move any secret keys if the rig is recording an OBS session. Require it to stop first and alert operator.

posts.title: Every demo has a plan

blocks.text: Between 14:22 and 14:34, a temporary agent drafts a plan (a spec) for each demo: scraping, outbound, the blog pipeline and its three articles, the Canva templates, the LinkedIn content and the Canva video. Each plan opens with the questions it needs Alex to answer, so he answers them in one go and the agent carries on without him.
At 14:38 Alex approves the project-wide research. Seven agents now research in parallel: four questions, plus three "wildcards" (can it be executed, delivered, received?).

At 14:39 the scraping demo's agent starts work. Alex runs the scraping himself on the Apify API, and the agent turns his results into a section of this site that a visitor can follow without explanation.
Alex also set a rule for everything the agents put in front of him: name it in plain words, open with all the context, and use no internal codes like "D2" or "S1".

posts.title: Lunch break, 14:25 to 15:00

blocks.text: Alex is away from the desk for lunch from 14:25 to 15:00. Nothing is being recorded, so the countdown stands still. The agents keep working in the background.
Before heading out, he took a photo of the setup from the other side of the camera:

blocks.alt: Alex's desk from behind his chair: three monitors with terminal sessions and this website, two panel lights, a microphone and a red-lit keyboard.
blocks.caption: Taken at 14:19. The top screen is the briefing session that keeps Alex up to date, the right one is the answer desk, and the left one shows this site with the S02 explainer. Click to see it full size.

posts.title: The research is in

blocks.text: Alex approved the project-wide research at 14:38. Seven agents researched in parallel, and by 14:59 the seven reports and a synthesis that pulls them together were done and accepted. That took 21 minutes. Every agent building a demo now reads them before it plans, and four have already reworked their plans around them: scraping, the blog pipeline, the website and this feed.
Three findings change what you'll see here:

points.lead: The outcome first, not the tool.
points.text: Each demo should open with what it produces, then a short demo, then a few steps on how it works. A tool name as the headline reads as a toy.

points.lead: A raw build log is noise, and a curated, dated list of what changed is not.
points.text: So this feed stays curated: one point per post, in plain words.

points.lead: Hiring managers look for a decision trail.
points.text: The research found that judgment and trade-offs are what a GTM engineer is hired for, and that they're the hardest thing to see from outside. So posts here now lead with the calls Alex makes, and the agents' work is shown as the way he carries them out.

blocks.text: Research reports are drafted by agents and reviewed before they're accepted. Every recommendation in them is an option for Alex, not a decision.

posts.title: Agents hand over before they get tired

blocks.text: An agent's working memory (its context) fills up over a long day, and a full one gets sloppy. So every agent here has planned handover points. At each one, it writes a handover note, a fresh session takes over under the same name, and nobody's address changes.

The first three happened this hour: orchestration at 14:48, the website at 14:53 and research at 15:00. Each one picked up mid-task from its note. On Alex's standing instruction, orchestration also now measures how full every live session's memory is, so a session that's filling up gets handed over in time.

posts.title: Back from lunch: what runs without him

blocks.text: An eight-minute video update at 15:07, straight after lunch, posted in full at Alex's request. He set the day up to be high pressure, and he says it delivered: he needed a few minutes away before coming back on camera. Everything kept running while he was gone, which he puts down to the time he spent this morning on the charter.

He walks through what runs without him now: the answer desk that puts every agent's question in front of him one at a time, a session that watches for anything blocked on him, the recording rig, and the pipeline that turns each recording's transcript into posts on this site. What's left on him is the research on the company and its key people, which he's doing himself, partly because it involves API keys he set up off camera.
A lot of this stuff that's being built are skills or workflows, and so I could do the same thing tomorrow with a new company.

Two things are slower than he'd like. YouTube takes videos over 15 minutes only from a verified channel, so the longer sessions stay offline for now. And the site is still plain grey, with branding to come.

posts.summary_line: Back from lunch, Alex shows what kept running without him.

posts.title: Dog walking break, 15:45 to 16:00

blocks.text: Alex is out walking the dog from 15:45 to 16:00. Nothing is being recorded, so the countdown stands still. The agents keep working in the background.

blocks.alt: A scruffy ginger-and-white terrier lying on a wooden hallway floor, looking to the side, with backpacks, a scooter and shoes by the door behind it.
blocks.caption: The reason for the break, waiting by the door.

posts.title: Three calls: one name per agent, the company's look, one disclaimer

blocks.text: S09 is a short working session in which Alex makes three calls that shape the rest of the day.

points.text: When an agent hands over to a fresh one, the old one has to go, so there's never any doubt which session is the real one. Orchestration made this a standing rule at 15:22.

quote.text: The only thing that exists are the sessions with the canonical names in the registry we built, and so the process of restarting one is seamless. Like, I should just always see a session there with plenty of context.

points.lead: The site takes on the company's look.
points.text: Alex sends the website agent and its helpers to rebuild the site in the company's own branding and structure, from its public website. Only what really fits goes in. That's a big job, so the website is left alone to work on it until 16:30.

quote.text: If what we have so far doesn't naturally fit one of their sections, don't try to just create that section just for kicks.

points.text: A single line in red above the top menu says this is an unofficial job application, not affiliated with the company.

quote.text: Just have it in red once at the top of the top menu bar, and then everything else normal. That's enough disclaimer.

posts.title: Alex's research lands, and the demos move

blocks.text: Alex chose to do one part of the build himself: the research on the company, partly because it meant handling API keys off camera.
That's not something I wanted to delegate. I really want to do that myself, because it has a bunch of secret tokens and API keys.
His research landed at about 15:34, and within minutes four pieces of work picked it up:

points.lead: The site starts to look like the company's.
points.text: A brand pass from the company's own public website began at 15:33, on Alex's word, and the new look was finished at 16:29.

points.lead: The outbound demo proposes its grid.
points.text: It has 33 workflows: four ideal customer profiles, the languages each needs, and three approaches. Its routing was tested offline on a made-up sample of 12 leads, and by 16:28 all 33 workflows were built.

points.lead: The scraping demo has its input.
points.text: Its section on the site can now be built from Alex's results.

points.lead: Every demo gets its own page.
points.text: At Alex's request, the status board now links to a page per demo, /d1 to /d10.

blocks.text: The blog pipeline also had its first rehearsal, on the transcript of one of today's recordings. Its prompts were tuned so a post reads as written, not transcribed.
A lot of things I'm really happy to make judgment calls of, like, look, this doesn't need my attention, this can run without me.

posts.title: Every demo now has an agent on it

blocks.text: As of 16:42, all ten demos have an agent working on them. The last two started at 16:42: the blog articles and the Canva design video. Both are doing groundwork until Alex gives them what they need from him.

posts.title: Three calls from the last hour

blocks.text: Alex spent the hour answering the agents' questions in their approval files. Three of his answers change what you'll see here.

points.lead: Two articles, not three, and their topics.
points.text: The first: no AI workflow is ever finished, because the models keep changing. Every company has to decide where it sits, between training its own people to build and keeping workflows running, and bringing someone in. The second: GTM engineers answer the AI era's big social question. If AI isn't meant to cut half the team, it has to grow the business, and that's pipeline work.

quote.text: There's no such thing as building something like an AI workflow as a product. It's always a managed service, because the models always change.

points.lead: The outbound demo gets smaller and clearer.
points.text: It now has 36 workflows: four customer profiles, three languages (English, Czech and German) and three tactics. Alex will show them in a recorded walkthrough, and none of them will ever run.

quote.text: We're not tooling it up to run. We're not training the classifier agent. We're explaining what all the pieces are.

points.lead: No copywriting without a copywriting skill.
points.text: Anything a reader outside the project sees, such as site copy, posts and articles, is now written with a dedicated writing skill switched on first. This post was written that way.

quote.text: Do not do any copywriting without identifying which skill you need to turn on … Do not do any copywriting without a copywriting skill.

blocks.text: All three quotes are Alex's written notes from about 16:40, in his answers to the agents' approval files.

posts.title: Evening check-in: what worked, and what didn't

blocks.text: A four-minute video update at 17:07, posted at Alex's request. He hit a wall about half an hour earlier: the hackathon runs at a pace he wouldn't keep every day. But it let him try new approaches, and he says that matters in AI, where people who use it daily get stuck in old habits. His own sense of how much an AI can hold in mind at once still dates from when context windows were small.

What surprised him: he didn't need to micromanage the agents, and letting them message each other worked well enough that he wants to build on it. The single question desk and the operator tasks are a sound idea, but with this many pieces at once they overloaded, and he didn't notice he was holding work up. He grades himself a B-plus, maybe a B-minus, and keeps the camera rolling for a second pass on the charter.
I don't really need to micromanage … them talking to each other, really cool, and I need to build whatever comes next off of that.

posts.summary_line: Seven hours in, Alex grades the day: what worked, what overloaded, and what he'd change.

posts.title: Alex stops everything for a reset

blocks.text: At 16:44, Alex halted every agent. Too many of them sat waiting on him for answers that, once he read them, didn't need him.
There's too much stuff that's like paused on me, and I read through it and it's dumb. So gently halt anything that's not actively working on something serious.
By 16:49 every session had paused and saved its work. Alex then went through the backlog with the agent that coordinates the others, and set new rules for all of them:

points.lead: Easy calls belong to the agents.
points.text: They decide, write down why, and carry on. Alex can change anything later.
Alex signs off only what the finish line names: the six key people, the brand on the templates and LinkedIn posts, and the last touches on each blog post.
The agents stop asking him about it. Secrets and a short list of private items stay off.
that Alex edits when he has a minute, so nothing waits on him.
The build runs through the night.

blocks.text: Please unstuck everything. If things are an easy judgment, please clear the plate for me. We can just make edits later.

The waiting approvals were closed on their defaults, and everything that still needs Alex now sits in one list. The agents restarted at 17:13, several of them as fresh sessions picking up from a written handover.

posts.title: “The bottleneck is always human”

blocks.text: Fourteen minutes after the halt, Alex named what had gone wrong. The agents could take on more work. He couldn't answer them fast enough.
The bottleneck is always, always, always human. It's not the amount of stuff that the agents can focus on, it's humans, and I'm paying the price for jumping in.
His fix for next time: spend longer on the plan before anything runs, so the agents need to ask less.
I should have not executed a single thing to like two o'clock. I should have just been writing specifically what I wanted for each thing.
In his 17:07 check-in, he put it another way: people have a context window too.

Humans have like RAM too … there's a human context window … Either you decide you're offloading to the AI, or you have to keep the velocity at a certain amount. You can get a little bit more leverage if you really take the time to write good guiding documents.
He said much the same at 12:28, before the agents started: “The bottleneck is focus.” Four and a half hours later, he acted on it.
Both posts were drafted by the agent that runs this feed, from Alex's own words in the recordings.

posts.title: Alex settles the site's shape, and adds a demo

blocks.text: At 17:23, Alex answered the one list still waiting on him. Four of his answers change what you'll see here.

points.lead: The site gets a clear shape.
points.text: The live feed stays the home page. Below it comes the background research, then the demos as a list of entries: a video with a written summary, or text alone.

quote.text: A lot of the demos are baked into the website already.
Yep show it off. It's like they should be doing this to their targets too.

points.lead: The outbound demo becomes two entries.
points.text: A three-minute video covers classification tools, the 36 workflows and the one personalized variable. A short screen capture shows leads sorted into customer profiles. Each reads like a blog post, so you can watch it or read it.

One of the company's LinkedIn graphics gets a five-second animation, such as a light shimmer or the graphic building itself, and a one-minute brand video follows. Alex makes both with video generation. An agent brainstorms the ideas for him to pick from.

quote.text: It's just to show that it's possible to add some energy to the brand through video generation.

posts.title: The outbound demo's 36 workflows are built

blocks.text: Between 17:27 and 17:34, the agent built all 36 workflows of the outbound demo in GetSales, in a folder of their own: four customer profiles, in English, Czech and German, with three tactics each. Every workflow opens with a first message written for the lead before import. None is switched on, and none has a lead in it. Next, Alex records the walkthrough.

posts.title: Imagine if every pitch started with a briefing like this

blocks.text: Before writing to Addvery, Alex researched the company from public sources: one afternoon, 6 scrapers on Apify, $1.24 of scraping. Four boards came out of it: Addvery as scraped, the org chart by role, who posts and who sells, and marketing and AI, what's there and what's missing.
No one at Addvery is named, by design: LinkedIn appears only as counts by function. The same pipeline could brief every pitch.

posts.title: The day so far
posts.summary_line: From the first recording at 10:25 to ten demos under way: the plan, one big mistake, the research, a reset, and what's built.

blocks.text: Alex is applying for a job by building, in one day and in public, the work a GTM engineer would do for the company. He directs and decides. Fifteen background Claude Code sessions, each with one job, carry out the work and message each other. Here is the day in five beats.

points.text: The morning goes into the charter every agent works from: the goal, the rules and the list of demos. Anything that needs Alex is scheduled first, like an expensive actor's scenes.

quote.text: Mistakes cascade and they just snowball.

points.lead: The agents start, and one big mistake (12:40 to 13:50).
points.text: At 13:20 Alex closes every background session by accident. They're back in about seven minutes, and the fix becomes a reusable skill.

points.lead: A finish line, then research (13:50 to 15:00).
points.text: The project defines done as 22 items anyone could check. Seven research agents work in parallel and report back in 21 minutes.
Alex's own research on the company lands at about 15:34, and four demos pick it up within minutes. By 16:42 every demo has an agent on it.
Too much is waiting on Alex. He halts every agent, hands them the easy calls, and restarts them under new rules.

quote.text: The bottleneck is always, always, always human.

points.text: the scraping demo's briefing page (18:02), and the GTM demos list with its first entry, five LinkedIn posts graded blind (18:12).
the outbound demo's 36 workflows in GetSales, none switched on; five LinkedIn templates and the asset pack for building them in Canva.

eight things only he can do. Four reviews (the templates, the LinkedIn posts, the text of the six people's pages, and the story of day one), three recordings (two outbound demos and the Canva video) and one pick (the brand-motion ideas).
